title: Australian Citizenship

exam.scoring: 75% required, all of the 5 values questions correct

content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public Australian citizenship test curriculum. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: In Australia, freedom of speech allows people to express their views openly, but that freedom does not protect speech that does what?
options: Breaks another law, such as by inciting violence or defaming a person
items.explanation: Australian law protects free expression, yet it does not permit speech that breaks other laws such as incitement to violence, while the other three options are lawful activities.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which statement best describes how democracy works in Australia?
options: The monarch personally writes every law
Citizens choose their government through free and fair elections
Only landowners are allowed to vote
Judges appoint the members of parliament
items.explanation: In an Australian democracy the people elect their representatives at free and fair elections, whereas the other options describe systems that do not operate in Australia.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: The Australian value of mutual respect requires people to treat others in which way?
options: With suspicion until they prove they are loyal
Only if they share the same religion
With dignity, including those who hold different views or beliefs
Only if they were born in Australia
items.explanation: Mutual respect means treating all people with dignity regardless of their background or opinions, so the conditional and exclusionary options contradict the value.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: What does the rule of law mean in Australia?
options: The police may ignore the law when they choose
Only judges are required to obey the law
Laws apply only to people who are not citizens
Everyone, including the government, is subject to the same laws
items.explanation: The rule of law means that every person and institution, including the government, must obey the law, while the other options would place someone above the law.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Freedom of religion in Australia means that people are free to do what?
options: Follow any religion, or no religion, without fear of persecution
Follow only the religion of the majority
Practise a religion only in private at home
Change their religion only with government approval
items.explanation: Australian values protect the right to follow any faith or none at all without persecution, whereas the other options impose restrictions that do not exist here.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which statement reflects the Australian value of equality between men and women?
options: Men should earn more than women for the same job
Men and women should have equal rights and opportunities in all aspects of life
Women should not serve in the armed forces
Only men should hold leadership positions
items.explanation: Gender equality means men and women share equal rights and opportunities, so the other options describe unequal treatment that Australian values reject.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: The Australian idea of a fair go is best described as which of the following?
options: Wealthy people should receive preferential treatment
Only some people deserve a second chance
Everyone deserves an equal opportunity to succeed regardless of background
Competition should be limited to one group
items.explanation: A fair go means giving everyone an equal opportunity based on merit rather than background, which is the opposite of the preferential treatment in the other options.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: In Australia, it is against the law to discriminate against a person because of which characteristic?
options: Their race, colour, religion or national origin
items.explanation: Australian anti-discrimination law prohibits unfair treatment based on protected attributes such as race, religion and national origin, not on personal preferences like sport or music.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: What does Australian law expect of every citizen regarding the law itself?
options: Citizens must obey the law and respect the rights of others
Citizens may break the law if they disagree with it
Only public servants must obey the law
Citizens must obey only the laws they voted for
items.explanation: All citizens are expected to obey the law and respect the rights of others, whereas the other options describe selective obedience that is contrary to the rule of law.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Freedom of assembly in Australia gives people the right to gather and protest in which manner?
options: Violently if the cause is considered important
Peacefully and lawfully, without harming others or damaging property
Only with written permission from a judge
Only if they belong to a registered political party
items.explanation: The right to assemble and protest is protected when it is peaceful and lawful, so the violent or heavily restricted alternatives are not consistent with Australian values.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Australian society values tolerance, which means what?
options: Requiring everyone to adopt the same culture
Banning the expression of minority opinions
Accepting and respecting people of different cultures and beliefs
Ignoring differences rather than acknowledging them
items.explanation: Tolerance means accepting and respecting cultural and religious diversity, while the other options describe forced conformity or suppression that contradicts the value.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Freedom of association in Australia allows people to do what?
options: Join only groups approved by the government
Belong to a single official organisation only
Form groups only for business purposes
Join or leave lawful groups and organisations of their choosing
items.explanation: Freedom of association lets people choose the lawful groups they join or leave, whereas the other options describe restrictions that Australian values do not permit.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which of these is a responsibility shared by Australian citizens called for jury service?
options: Serving on a jury when summoned by the court
Paying a fee to avoid jury duty
Choosing which trial to sit on
Deciding the sentence for a convicted person
items.explanation: Citizens may be summoned to serve on a jury, and the judge, not the juror, decides the sentence, so the other options misdescribe the jury system.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Respect for the law in Australia helps to achieve which outcome?
options: An orderly and fair society where rights are protected
items.explanation: Respecting the law underpins an orderly society that protects everyone's rights, while the remaining options are unrelated to or contrary to that purpose.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: How are Australian citizens expected to take part in their democracy?
options: By leaving all decisions to public servants
By voting in elections and keeping informed about public issues
By voting only in local elections
items.explanation: Active participation through voting and staying informed is expected of citizens, whereas the other options describe passive or incomplete ways of taking part.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which of the following actions best reflects the value of helping your community in Australia?
options: Moving away whenever a problem arises
Volunteering time to support local people and services
items.explanation: Contributing to the community through volunteering reflects shared civic responsibility, while the other options describe withdrawal from or neglect of the community.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: In Australia, the right to free expression is balanced against which obligation?
options: Respecting the rights and reputation of other people
Never disagreeing with a public official
items.explanation: Free expression must be balanced with respect for the rights and reputation of others, and the other options would wrongly restrict the right itself.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which value is demonstrated when an Australian respects a person's right to hold an opinion different from their own?
options: Agreement with the majority at all times
Mutual respect and tolerance for differing views
items.explanation: Respecting the right to differ reflects mutual respect and tolerance, whereas the other options describe conformity, indifference or obedience rather than genuine respect.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: What does Australia's commitment to equality require of its citizens and government?
options: Treating all people fairly and without discrimination
Applying the law differently by gender
items.explanation: Equality requires fair treatment of all people without discrimination, so the other options describe preferential or discriminatory treatment that Australia rejects.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: Which behaviour is consistent with the Australian value of obeying the law?
options: Copying the behaviour of a crowd breaking the law
Paying taxes and following road rules
items.explanation: Paying taxes and following road rules are examples of lawful behaviour expected of everyone, while the other options describe unlawful conduct.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Values

items.stem: In which year did the Australian colonies unite to form the Commonwealth of Australia?
items.explanation: The colonies federated and the Commonwealth of Australia came into being on 1 January 1901, while 1770 and 1788 relate to early British contact and settlement.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are recognised as having which distinction?
options: Arriving in Australia in the twentieth century
The oldest continuous cultures in the world
The first Europeans to settle the continent
Originating from the Pacific islands only
items.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples hold the world's oldest continuous cultures, so the other options misstate their origins and history.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Which explorer claimed the east coast of Australia for Britain in 1770?
items.explanation: Captain James Cook charted and claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770, while Flinders, Banks and Stirling played different later roles.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: The First Fleet arrived in Australia in 1788 at which location?
options: Sydney Cove in New South Wales
items.explanation: The First Fleet landed at Sydney Cove in 1788, and the other locations were the sites of later settlements in the other colonies.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: On what date did the Australian Constitution take effect?
items.explanation: The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901 when the colonies federated, whereas the other dates mark unrelated historical events.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Who is Australia's head of state?
options: The King, represented in Australia by the Governor-General
The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Chief Justice of the High Court
items.explanation: The King is Australia's head of state and is represented by the Governor-General, while the Prime Minister leads the government rather than serving as head of state.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: The Parliament of Australia consists of which components?
options: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet only
The King, the Senate and the House of Representatives
The High Court and the Governor-General only
items.explanation: Australia's Federal Parliament comprises the King (through the Governor-General), the Senate and the House of Representatives, not the bodies in the other options.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: In the Australian Parliament, how many senators does each state elect?
items.explanation: Each of the six states elects twelve senators, while the territories elect fewer, so the other figures do not match the constitutional arrangement.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Voting in Australian federal elections is described by which rule?
options: Voting is compulsory for eligible citizens aged 18 and over
items.explanation: Eligible citizens aged 18 and over must vote at federal elections, and the other options describe rules that do not apply in Australia.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Which court is the highest court in the Australian judicial system?
options: The Supreme Court of New South Wales
items.explanation: The High Court of Australia is the nation's highest court and interprets the Constitution, while the other courts operate at state or lower federal levels.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: The separation of powers in Australia divides government authority among which three branches?
options: The federal, state and local governments
The Senate, the Cabinet and the police
The legislature, the executive and the judiciary
The monarch, the army and the public service
items.explanation: The separation of powers divides authority among the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, whereas the other options confuse different concepts such as levels of government.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: How can the Australian Constitution be changed?
options: By a simple vote in the House of Representatives
By a decision of the Governor-General alone
By a ruling of the High Court
Through a referendum approved by a majority of voters in a majority of states
items.explanation: Changing the Constitution requires a referendum with a double majority, so the other options describe mechanisms that cannot amend it.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: In the Australian system of government, who becomes Prime Minister?
options: The leader of the party that wins a majority of seats in the House of Representatives
A person directly elected by all voters
The Governor-General's chosen adviser without regard to parliament
items.explanation: The Prime Minister is the leader who commands a majority in the House of Representatives, rather than being directly elected or chosen without parliamentary support.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: What are the three levels of government in Australia?
options: Federal, state or territory, and local
items.explanation: Australia has federal, state or territory, and local levels of government, while the other groupings either no longer exist or describe arms of a single level.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: What was the significance of the 1967 referendum?
options: It allowed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to be counted in the census and for the Commonwealth to make laws for them
items.explanation: The 1967 referendum enabled Indigenous Australians to be counted in the census and empowered the Commonwealth to legislate for them, unlike the other unrelated changes.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: The High Court's 1992 Mabo decision was significant because it did what?
options: Recognised native title rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
items.explanation: The Mabo decision recognised native title in Australian law, whereas the other outcomes were not results of that landmark case.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: How many states and mainland territories make up the Commonwealth of Australia?
options: Six states and two mainland territories
items.explanation: Australia has six states and two mainland territories, so the other combinations do not match the actual federal structure.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Australia's method of voting, which uses a private booth and a printed ballot, is widely known as what?
options: The secret ballot, or Australian ballot
items.explanation: Australia pioneered the secret ballot, where votes are cast privately, unlike the open or restricted methods in the other options.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: What role does the Governor-General perform in relation to laws passed by Parliament?
options: Writing the text of every bill
Giving royal assent so that a bill becomes law
items.explanation: The Governor-General grants royal assent for bills to become law, while the other options describe powers that are not part of that ceremonial and constitutional role.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: Anzac Day, observed on 25 April, commemorates which group?
options: The members of the High Court
Australians and New Zealanders who served in wars and peacekeeping
items.explanation: Anzac Day honours Australians and New Zealanders who served in wars and peacekeeping, rather than settlers, federation founders or judges.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australia's History and Government

items.stem: What is the capital city of Australia?
items.explanation: Canberra is the national capital, while Sydney, Melbourne and Perth are capitals of individual states rather than of the nation.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which Australian state is the largest by area?
items.explanation: Western Australia covers the greatest land area of any state, larger than Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which Australian state is the smallest by area?
items.explanation: Tasmania is the smallest state by area, being an island, whereas Victoria and the other mainland states are larger.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: What are the official national colours of Australia?
items.explanation: Australia's national colours are green and gold, recalling the golden wattle, while the other combinations are not the official national colours.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which flower is Australia's national floral emblem?
items.explanation: The golden wattle is the national floral emblem, and the other flowers, while native, are not the official national flower.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which two animals commonly appear on the Australian coat of arms?
items.explanation: The kangaroo and the emu, chosen partly because they are seen as unable to walk backwards, support the shield on the coat of arms.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which symbol appears in the top-left corner of the Australian national flag?
items.explanation: The Union Jack occupies the top-left quarter of the flag, while the Southern Cross and Commonwealth Star appear in other positions.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: On the Australian flag, what does the large Commonwealth Star represent?
options: The six states and the territories
items.explanation: The seven-pointed Commonwealth Star represents the six states and the territories, while the smaller stars represent the Southern Cross.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Which constellation is shown on the Australian national flag?
items.explanation: The Southern Cross appears on the flag as a group of stars, whereas the other constellations are not featured on it.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: What is the national anthem of Australia?
items.explanation: Advance Australia Fair is the national anthem, while Waltzing Matilda is an unofficial folk song and the others are not the current anthem.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: What is the official currency of Australia?
items.explanation: Australia uses the Australian dollar, which replaced the Australian pound in 1966, so the other currencies are not in use.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: What is the highest mountain on the Australian mainland?
items.explanation: Mount Kosciuszko in the Snowy Mountains is the highest peak on the mainland, while the other peaks are lower or located elsewhere.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: In which state is the Great Barrier Reef located?
items.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of Queensland, not off New South Wales, Western Australia or Tasmania.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: In which territory is Uluru located?
items.explanation: Uluru is located in the Northern Territory, while the Australian Capital Territory and the other states are different jurisdictions.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Sydney is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Sydney is the capital of New South Wales, whereas Melbourne, Brisbane and Hobart are the capitals of Victoria, Queensland and Tasmania.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Melbourne is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Melbourne is the capital of Victoria, while the other states have their own capital cities such as Sydney, Adelaide and Perth.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Brisbane is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, whereas the capitals of the other states listed are Sydney, Melbourne and Hobart.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Perth is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Perth is the capital of Western Australia, while Adelaide, Brisbane and Sydney are the capitals of the other states mentioned.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Adelaide is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, whereas Melbourne, Perth and Hobart are the capitals of the other states listed.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols

items.stem: Hobart is the capital city of which Australian state?
items.explanation: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania, and the other states named have different capitals such as Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.
items.reference: Australian Citizenship Test Curriculum - Australian Geography and Symbols
